source_entries.source_observation: computability and the halting structure -- bounded decidable, the unbounded limit undecidable. Phase XII (mathematics itself), target four, forward from the bounded-denominator finite-configuration mechanism (G10/G14) and the continuum wall (G10). A fold-process on bounded denominators lives in a finite state space, because the bounded-denominator configurations are finite in number. A process confined to a finite state space must, by the pigeonhole principle, either halt or repeat a state and so enter a cycle, and which of these it does is decidable: one runs it and watches, and within the finite count of available states it must either stop or revisit a state already seen, settling whether it halts. So on bounded denominators the halting question is decidable, and the fold-process is a perfectly well-behaved finite computation. The undecidable cases, where the halting problem genuinely bites, are the unbounded limit: when denominators are permitted to grow without bound the state space becomes infinite, the continuum-like wall, and a process can run forever without ever repeating a state, so no general decision procedure can exist. The boundary of decidability is therefore exactly the boundary between the bounded and the unbounded, between the finite fold-space and the continuum limit, the same wall that appears throughout the framework. Falsification condition (the derivation stands on the One; this is only what observation would have to show to contradict it): an undecidable halting question on a genuinely bounded finite space, or decidable halting on the full unbounded space, would break the result. External correspondence (what the derived result agrees with, never what makes it true): the halting problem and the decidability boundary [Turing's halting problem; the decidability of finite-state machines; the finite-versus-infinite boundary]. The standard account separates finite automata, which are decidable, from Turing machines with unbounded tape, which are not; the framework proves this same split as the bounded-versus-unbounded denominator boundary.
